newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CONTRASTING STYLES FOR FERGUSON AND EVANS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CONTRASTING STYLES FOR FERGUSON AND EVANS.

text.p: Alex Ferguson and Roy Evans both manage soccer clubs. But that is where the resemblance ends.
For while Manchester United boss Ferguson is famous for his mind-games, trying to psyche out the opposition especially when the pressure is on, Liverpool manager Evans follows a quieter path.
Since taking over from Graeme Souness three years ago, he has re-fashioned Liverpool in his own understated, yet effective, style.
Indeed the influential magazine Four Four Two once dubbed him: "The Invisible Manager."

Evans had been in control at Anfield for less than a year at the time, and to call him that now would be unfair. Everyone who follows football knows who Evans is. He would just prefer you did not make too much fuss about it.

Which is one reason why the current spat between the two managers, plus Arsenal's Arsene Wenger, over allowing Manchester United more time to finish their fixtures with an extension to the season, is so unusual.
Evans does not usually get drawn into those kind of rows in public. In fact, he'd rather not row in private either if he could help it.

"I always try to be fair," he says, "and I would much rather solve a problem logically and rationally than shouting about it. Of course, that's not always possible, but it's the way I like to do things."

Evans, 45, has been at Liverpool for 30 years since Bill Shankly signed him as a 15-year-old apprentice. An England Schoolboy international, he had talent, but lacked pace and after playing only 11 times for Liverpool's first team in five years, the then manager Bob Paisley suggested he retire as a player and concentrate on coaching.

He was an almost immediate success, managing the reserves from 1974 until 1983, and then coaching the first team until May 1993 when he became assistant manager, taking over as manager from Graeme Souness in January 1994. The appointment was met in the media with cries of "Roy Who?" but once again the club knew what they were doing.

Dapper, silver-haired, urbane and usually obliging with his time for an interview or chat, Evans has re-fashioned Liverpool in the image of Shankly, Paisley and Dalglish. They play with flair and style, and are close to becoming champions again.
Whether they do that this season or not will depend greatly on the outcome of Saturday's match.
In some ways, Evans is now where Ferguson was in 1989. After three seasons at Old Trafford, Ferguson's United had finished 11th, 2nd and 11th in the league and had won no major trophies.

But the diligent and hard-working Ferguson had laid the groundwork for the success that has come in the 1990s. In 1990 United won the FA Cup, and have since won eight trophies including the Cup and league double twice.

While Liverpool-born Evans has stuck to his roots, spending 30 years at Anfield, Ferguson has remained close to his roots, although his playing and coaching career has embraced nine clubs and great success in both Scotland and England.
Ferguson remains closely involved in helping deprived youngsters in the tough working-class Glasgow district of Govan where he grew up, an area now decimated by the loss of industry in the area.

And despite the wealth he has earned since taking United to the heights of success, he has remained a loyal socialist at heart, actively supporting the Labour candidate at the last local elections in Glasgow.
Despite their different personalities and backgrounds, both men could yet be united in celebration next month. Liverpool could win the title, United the European Cup.
There is also the possibility that Ferguson could be celebrating a double of the English title and European Cup, and even a treble if Labour win the British General Election.
Whatever the outcome, Ferguson will probably go on being successful and making headlines at United for as long as he is boss there.
And Evans will continue to plot his revolution at Anfield. Quietly, and without too much fuss.
